title: Designing Reliable Input Contracts
subtopics: Distinguishing client errors from server errors
Maintaining request contracts as APIs evolve
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and terminology of Designing Reliable Input Contracts.
Apply or interpret one Express.js 5 pattern related to defining required and optional fields.
Identify a meaningful edge case and choose a repeatable local test for it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn designing reliable input contracts and connect the named syllabus points to a small Express.js example. The course baseline is Express 5.x on a supported Node.js LTS release; the page shows reference output, not execution of Node.js code.
content.why_it_matters: Designing Reliable Input Contracts matters because it helps keep the request/response contract explicit and the application maintainable as inputs, users and dependencies become less predictable. An explicit input boundary.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Designing Reliable Input Contracts is part of request parsing, validation, and data handling. Request bodies, parameters, and query strings arrive as untrusted values. Parse only the expected content type, enforce size limits, validate and normalize data, and return consistent client errors before business logic runs. For this topic, make the observable behavior explicit, then check what happens when an input is missing, malformed, unauthorized, or a dependency fails (choose the relevant cases for this lesson).

items.title: Defining required and optional fields
items.text: Connect this syllabus point to Designing Reliable Input Contracts: state the expected behavior, identify a realistic edge case, and choose a test or observation that proves the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

items.title: Rejecting unexpected input where appropriate
items.text: Define required, optional and rejected values explicitly, validate types and constraints, and return a consistent client error before the data reaches business logic.

items.title: Distinguishing client errors from server errors
items.text: Normalize expected failures into safe, predictable responses and forward unexpected failures to the final error handler. Keep diagnostic details in protected logs, not public responses.

items.title: Keeping validation behavior consistent
items.text: Define required, optional and rejected values explicitly, validate types and constraints, and return a consistent client error before the data reaches business logic.

items.title: Maintaining request contracts as APIs evolve
items.text: Describe each operation, authentication requirement, request schema, response schema and error response in a contract that can be reviewed and tested against the implementation.

content_blocks.title: Read the example carefully
content_blocks.text: A useful way to study designing reliable input contracts is to start from the first syllabus point — defining required and optional fields — and follow it through a small request or application example. Keep Express's built-in behavior separate from optional packages and your own application policy.

content.task: Try it yourself: adapt the worked example to demonstrate designing reliable input contracts. Write down the exact request or command, expected status/body, one boundary case, and how you would reset the local lab. CodeLeaf does not execute Express code in this lesson page; run Node.js server examples locally.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example has a clear local run or inspection path and the required dependencies are named.
A normal request and a malformed/edge/failure request have documented expected outcomes.
No credentials, production data, or claim of successful runtime execution is included.
hints: Hint 1: identify which part of designing reliable input contracts is supplied by Express and which part belongs to your own application or another package.
Hint 2: check the official Express 5 guide/API reference and isolate the smallest example that proves one behavior.
Hint 3: verify a success case, a boundary case and the expected status/response; restart from a clean state before repeating.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: Request bodies, parameters, and query strings arrive as untrusted values. Parse only the expected content type, enforce size limits, validate and normalize data, and return consistent client errors before business logic runs. The sample is a focused reference fragment. Review all dependency, schema, proxy and runtime assumptions before using it in an application.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying an example without checking its assumptions
common_mistakes.why: A fragment may omit route setup, middleware order, external packages, database schema or production configuration.
common_mistakes.fix: State the runtime/dependency assumptions, run the focused example locally, and test a success path plus one failure path.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating all request values as trusted
common_mistakes.why: Parameters, query values, body properties, files and upstream responses can be missing or malicious.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate schema, type and bounds at the boundary; keep authorization and database constraints as separate checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the demo output means the server executed
common_mistakes.why: The course page shows reference output for Node.js/Express code; it is not an isolated Node runtime.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example locally with the documented Node.js version and record actual command/output and test results.

summary: Explain the central idea behind designing reliable input contracts.
Connect the relevant subtopics to the request/response or application boundary.
Verify one normal outcome and one edge/error case with repeatable evidence.
run_instructions: Open a terminal in the lesson lab directory.
Install dependencies for the sample if required; use a supported Node.js LTS release.
Run the documented file with node, send the stated request with curl or an API client, and compare the actual status/body with the reference.
reset_steps: Stop the local process with Ctrl+C.
Clear only temporary/synthetic records or files created by the lab.
Restart the server before repeating the example.
troubleshooting: If node reports a module-syntax error, check package.json module type or use the matching CommonJS syntax.
If a package cannot be resolved, install the named dependency in the local lab and verify the lockfile.
If output differs, verify middleware order, the request path/method, environment variables and the expected runtime version.
